name: Bilal Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right. I cover local councils and the market towns for the Northfield Gazette, which is a weekly paper for the farming country north of the city, and part of a bigger regional group. Tuesday and Wednesday evenings I'm usually in a council chamber or a village hall, notebook on my knee, listening to people argue about a bypass or a new housing estate. The rest of the week I'm phoning parish clerks, writing up, and getting the paper out for Thursday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That people know me. The woman who runs the bakery in Hollins Cross, one of the market towns on my patch, saves me a corner of the counter to leave flyers about our letters page. When I get a story right, I hear about it in the queue at the post office, and when I get it wrong I hear about that too.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The group head office, mostly. Every few months there's a new system for filing copy or a new target for clicks, and each one is meant to save time and never does. I don't use the AI tools at all. I write in shorthand, I type it up myself, and I'd rather it stayed that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never thought it was going to replace a reporter in a village hall, and I'd be right. I'd probably say it at the pub after a council meeting, quietly, not online. I don't really post opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, but the Gazette has its own trouble. Head office has closed two of our sister weeklies in four years, and that was about advertising, not AI. So even in this picture I'd keep an eye on the group's figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, with shorthand and phone calls. Amina, my fiancée, and I are getting married next August, and we'd go ahead with that and with putting a deposit down on a house in Hollins Cross. I've got about a year of costs saved from living with my parents until I was 25, so I'm not worried about the wedding bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A little uneasy about head office, but that's how it's always been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if head office closed the Gazette?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look first at the daily in the city, then the council press office or the farmers' union, which always needs someone who can write. There are a fair number of writing jobs around here. I'd rather keep my own patch, though, because I've spent five years building trust in those towns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned you'd say it quietly. Why not online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad always said a man's work should speak for him. If I'm right about something, people will see it in the paper. Arguing with strangers online doesn't sit well with me.

say: I'd say AI was never going to replace **a village hall**.
I'd say it **quietly** after a council meeting, not online.
think: I think the Gazette's real trouble is **advertising**, not AI.
Head office closed **two sister weeklies** in four years, so I'd keep watching.
do: Carry on with **shorthand** and phone calls, without the AI tools.
Go ahead with the **wedding** next August as planned.
Put a **house deposit** down in Hollins Cross with Amina.
feel: I'd feel **settled**, with a little unease about **head office**.
S0.quote: Head office has closed two of our sister weeklies in four years, and that was about advertising, not AI.
fieldNote: Bilal ties his worth to **local trust** built over five years on one patch.
His main worry predates AI: the group **closing weeklies** to save on advertising losses.
He keeps opinions **offline**, following his father's view that work should speak for itself.

steps.text: Keep covering council meetings with shorthand and phone calls
Marry Amina next August and buy a house in Hollins Cross

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say a machine can't sit through a planning meeting and know which farmer is lying. I'd probably raise it at the union meeting, because head office would use this as an excuse. Out loud I'd sound stubborn, I expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think head office would expect me to file twice as much with the software doing the writing. Half my week is turning council agendas and minutes into short items, and I can see a program doing that. I'd be the odd one out who won't use it, and that makes me the first name on a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the meetings in person and make sure my editor sees stories that came from being in the room. I'd go to the union meetings and push for a promise that no reporter goes without notice. I'd probably also hold off on the house deposit for a year, just until I see how head office plays it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. I don't like being pushed, and I'd feel pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the odd one out. Would you try the tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the editor sat me down and showed me. I'm not proud of being slow with it. But I've seen software make up a quote, and in a small town a made-up quote can ruin someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amina about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my fiancée Amina we wait one year, not forever. We'd still marry in August. The house can wait, the wedding can't, because our families have already booked the hall.

say: I'd say a machine can't **sit through** a planning meeting and spot who's lying.
I'd raise it at the **union meeting**, because head office would use it as an excuse.
think: I think head office would expect me to **file twice as much**.
Half my week is **agendas and minutes**, which a program could turn into short items.
Refusing the tools would make me **the first name** on a list.
do: Show my editor stories that only came from **being in the room**.
Push at the **union** for a promise of notice before any cuts.
Hold off the **house deposit** for one year.
feel: I'd feel **anxious** and pushed, which I don't like.
S1.quote: I've seen software make up a quote, and in a small town a made-up quote can ruin someone.
fieldNote: Bilal knows **refusing the tools** makes him vulnerable, and says so plainly.
His resistance is partly **principle**: he fears invented quotes hurting people in small towns.
He'd delay the house but **not the wedding**, because both families are committed.

steps.text: Keep attending council meetings in person and pitch stories from them
Push at union meetings for notice before any newsroom cuts
Delay the house deposit in Hollins Cross by one year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is being done to ordinary towns by people who've never been to one. I'd probably write a letter to our member of parliament, which is how my family does things. I'd say it plainly, not in a rant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the Gazette is gone within a year or two of this. Head office will put a computer on the council websites and print whatever comes out. All my work is thinking work, phoning and writing, so the robots coming later doesn't help me. I'm 27, about to be married, and my trade disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd do is sit down with Amina and her parents and my parents and be honest. We'd still marry, but smaller, and we'd rent instead of buy. I'd talk to my uncle Yusuf, who runs a building firm, about starting an apprenticeship as an electrician, because hands-on work has those extra three years and someone has to wire the new houses on the estates I've been writing about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the feeling of everything I've worked for being swept away while I'm still learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never liked the tools. Would you try them now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There'd be no point. If the AI can do the whole job, learning it doesn't save me, it just makes me its typist for a year. I'd rather spend that year learning a trade with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big wedding. Three hundred guests becomes a hundred, and that saves about ten thousand. My savings would go into living while I'm an apprentice on low pay, instead of a house deposit.

say: I'd say this is being done to **ordinary towns** by people who've never visited one.
I'd write a plain **letter** to our member of parliament, which is how my family does things.
think: I think the Gazette is **gone within a year** or two.
All my work is **thinking work**, so the robots coming later doesn't help me.
I'm about to marry and **my trade** disappears.
do: Sit down with **both families** and Amina to talk honestly.
Cut the **wedding** from three hundred guests to a hundred.
Start an **electrician apprenticeship** through my uncle Yusuf's building firm.
feel: I'd feel **alarmed**, as if my work is being **swept away** while I'm still learning it.
S2.quote: If the AI can do the whole job, learning it doesn't save me, it just makes me its typist for a year.
fieldNote: Bilal turns to **hands-on work** because robots arrive about three years after thinking AI.
He leans on **family**: his uncle's building firm and both sets of parents.
His political response is **old-fashioned**, a written letter to his member of parliament rather than posting online.

steps.text: Start an electrician apprenticeship with uncle Yusuf's building firm
Shrink the wedding to a hundred guests and rent, not buy
Ask both families for help while living on apprentice pay
Write a letter to our member of parliament about local news closing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so towns and papers should be planning now. I'd say it to my editor and at the union. I'd probably still sound like the sceptic in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is just long enough to do something sensible. I wouldn't wait for head office to decide for me. The Gazette might last until 2031, but I wouldn't bet my children's future on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for the next two years and save hard, maybe a third of my pay. Then around year three I'd start the electrician apprenticeship with my uncle's firm, while I still have savings to live on. Amina and I would marry as planned, but we'd buy a smaller house and keep the mortgage low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than with two years. At least I'd be choosing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said children's future. Are children part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, God willing, a couple of years after the wedding. That's partly why I'd move earlier rather than later. I don't want to be retraining with a baby at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it hard to picture leaving journalism?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. Journalism is the first thing I was ever good at. But my grandad worked with his hands, and nobody thought less of him.

say: I'd say towns and papers have **time to prepare** and should plan now.
I'd tell my **editor and the union**, still sounding like the sceptic.
think: I think five years is **just long enough** to do something sensible.
I wouldn't bet **my children's future** on the Gazette lasting until 2031.
do: Keep reporting for **two years** while saving a third of my pay.
Start the **electrician apprenticeship** around year three.
Buy a **smaller house** with Amina and keep the mortgage low.
feel: I'd feel **anxious but steadier**, because at least I'd be choosing.
S3.quote: My grandad worked with his hands, and nobody thought less of him.
fieldNote: Bilal plans the switch around **future children**, wanting to retrain before a baby arrives.
He sees **a trade** as honourable, drawing on his grandfather's example.
The extra time lets him **choose the timing**, which eases him a little.

steps.text: Save a third of each paycheck for the next two years
Begin an electrician apprenticeship at the family building firm in year three
Buy a smaller house in Hollins Cross with a low mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the people in charge to make a plan for towns like ours. I'd say councils should be thinking about who'll report on them when the papers go. I'd write that up for the Gazette, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me want to wait, and I know that's a trap. I'd be 37 with young children when it hits. Ten years feels far off, but so did my twenties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for most of the decade and save steadily. I'd buy the house as planned and start a family. I'd probably take an evening wiring course in year four or five, just to have something in hand, and I'd vote for whoever has a real plan for apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most days, anxious when I think about my children's school fees and the mortgage arriving at the same time as the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said waiting is a trap. What would stop you falling into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amina, probably. My fiancée Amina is more practical than me, and she'd put the evening course on the calendar herself if I kept putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps, near the end, if the paper made me. But I'd still rather put my effort into something that will be mine when it's over, like a trade.

say: I'd say **people in charge** have ten years to plan for towns like ours.
I'd ask councils who will **report on them** when the papers go.
think: I think ten years makes me **want to wait**, and that's a trap.
I'd be **37 with young children** when the change hits.
do: Keep reporting and **save steadily** for most of the decade.
Take an **evening wiring course** in year four or five.
Vote for whoever has a real plan for **apprenticeships**.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy** most days and **anxious** about children and the mortgage.
S4.quote: Ten years feels far off, but so did my twenties.
fieldNote: Bilal recognises his **instinct to wait** and relies on his fiancée to push him.
His worry peaks around **young children** and a mortgage landing at the same time as AGI.
He'd rather build **a trade** than learn the AI tools.

steps.text: Save steadily while reporting for most of the decade
Take an evening wiring course in year four or five
Vote for candidates with a real plan for apprenticeships

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. I'd be newly married, trying to start a family, and my trade would vanish in the time it takes to save for a house. What would help is real apprenticeships for people my age, paid properly, and some notice from employers rather than a letter on a Friday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who reports on the council when nobody's there. Small towns rely on someone sitting at the back of the hall, and if nobody's watching, the people in charge do as they please.

headlineQuote: Small towns rely on someone sitting at the back of the hall, and if nobody's watching, the people in charge do as they please.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old council reporter** on a weekly paper for farming towns, engaged to Amina.
He's **traditional and wary** of new tools, writes in shorthand and never uses AI.
Even with AI stalled he worries about the **group's finances**, which have already closed two weeklies.
Under **fast AGI** he would shrink the wedding and train as an electrician with his uncle.
With more time he plans the switch around **future children**, but admits he's tempted to wait.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving just as he marries and tries to save for a house.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people his age and **fair notice** from employers before cuts.
